newsitem.title: GERMANY: ALLIANZ TARGETS GLOBAL INDUSTRIAL INSURANCE.
newsitem.headline: ALLIANZ TARGETS GLOBAL INDUSTRIAL INSURANCE.

text.p: Allianz AG Holding aims to increase its global industrial business to three billion marks by 1998 or 1999 from two billion marks premium income now.

"We have a market share of between two and three percent. We want to double that in the foreseeable future," said Manfred Illner, president of Allianz Global Risk Management, in an interview with Reuters.
Already nearly all of the world's bottling plants for Coca-Cola, that most American of all American products, are insured by Allianz.
The deal with the beverage producer is a prime example of how global insurance programmes should operate, said Illner.
"Leading company is Allianz Insurance Company in Burbank, California. All Allianz companies and offices worldwide provide the local service for the Coca-Cola account, including us here in Germany."
The latest contract with Coca-Cola is for a global multi-line, multi-year programme.
Allianz is currently undergoing a fundamental reorganisation of its international industrial and commercial business to win more such lucrative deals.

Although international programmes form only a small part of Allianz's global 1996 income of 74.6 billion marks, and roughly half of its four billion marks total industrial business, Illner believes this sector has great potential - especially as it is very profitable.
Illner sees U.S. insurer AIG, Winterthur, Zurich and Gerling as his major competitors on a global scale.

Lloyd's was not sufficiently centrally organised to make an impact with such programmes, while others were not big enough. "We are among the top four in the world in this field. But we are sure that we are number one soon," he added.
The reorganisation is considerably tightening Allianz's central control over the international industrial business of local subsidiaries and offices.

Allianz used to have an international board for international industrial insurance, which led a separate international department. This provided consulting and reinsurance services in international industrial cover to group members outside Germany, such as AIC in the U.S., Cornhill in the UK or RAS in Italy.

"Now, we have introduced a steering committee for all international industrial business. It consists of leading managers from the main group companies and will have strategic and operational leadership functions," Illner said.

The committee is headed by Reiner Hagemann, chief executive of Allianz's German property and casualty operations. Illner is the manager of the steering committee as well as of the whole organisation, which operates internationally under the name of Allianz Global Risk Division.
The former international department was merged with the industrial lines division of Allianz Versicherungs-AG and moved into a separate building at Munich's Leopoldstrasse.
"Instead of 35, there are now 160 people available for this international business," said Illner. "We have a much stronger focus on strategic planning and product development."
There would be a uniform corporate design and product strategy, a global marketing approach, worldwide training for underwriters and risk managers, and a new international liability strategy.

The group's newly-set-up ART unit dealing with alternative risk transfer is headed by Allianz board member Detlev Bremkamp, but close links between ART and the Global Risk Division have been formalised.
The ART company, which also does traditional active reinsurance, is based in Zurich, with offices in Rotterdam and New York.
Similarly close ties also exist with the Allianz centre for technology. "The centre will play an important role in the development of new industrial products," said Illner.
Property and casualty markets worldwide totalled 1,229 billion marks in 1995, he noted. Of that, some 57 percent were personal lines, 43 percent industrial and commercial.

Excluding small commercial and national commercial business, there was a target market of international and large national accounts with an estimated annual premium volume of 88 billion to 111 billion marks.

Allianz has introduced a nominated clients (NC) system. "We have a total of 1,068 nominated clients, which either have business with us already or which we want to have as clients. Of those 1,068, 671 have an international insurance programme (IIP) with us."

The emphasis is clearly on Germany. "Here, 279 NCs are based, 228 already with an international programme run by us. In the U.S., the NC figure is 260, of those, 110 are already on board," said Illner.

Allianz Cornhill has 141 nominated clients, 131 of them with IIP. In terms of premium income, too, Germany is still Allianz's largest market - international programmes yielded 1.18 billion marks in 1995, out of a total of 2.01 billion marks worldwide, followed by North America with 413 million marks and 370 million marks in Europe outside Germany.
Illner believes that Asia will be a key growth market for the future, although with just 40 million marks international programme business, Allianz still has some way to go.
The more centralised structure of the industrial division has not replaced the idea of local profit centres. "Each of our local units is responsible for its own results," he said.
"The international unit has to co-ordinate and to do the controlling. We also do the global marketing."

But what happens if a local Allianz company says that it cannot take a certain risk at the globally agreed rate? "It must accept the risk. But in such a case, we take the whole business as reinsurance. The local company is responsible for its net result, this is not affected."
Illner is well aware that Allianz's structure of local companies with responsibility for their results differs from the more central approach of rivals.
"Others don't have as much local know-how as we have. And we believe we have cured the problem of a possible lack of central control."
In the U.S., Allianz will aim particularly at the liability market. "So far, we have concentrated on property. We have now added more manpower in liability underwriting."

Illner believes that international insurance programmes have a great future. "The customer can bundle everything, this means considerable cost savings. Some large corporations have several programmes, one for each division."
Deductibles in international programmes now amount to between one or two million marks and 50 million marks. "For German corporations, 30 million marks has so far been the largest deductible."

The competitive situation of industrial insurers and reinsurers will change, Illner said. "Reinsurers will seek new areas of business, whether we like it or not. We are not unduly worried, as we also do some reinsurance."
-- Herbert Fromme, Reuters Insurance News +49 221 512007
